  history     0.35   accumulated message stream
  shell       0.30   cargo / gh / git command outputs
  filereads   0.20   Read tool calls returning file contents
  search      0.15   grep / find / glob in agent loops

Weights reflect this repo's observed shape — adjust for your
own workload via:

    --weights "history=0.4,shell=0.35,filereads=0.15,search=0.10"

## What this gives users

A single number to point at when asked "what does Sophon do on a
real Claude Code session?" — **~85 % across the typical mix of
tool traffic** — that's NOT cherry-picked from one bench but
blended from four independent measurements on real data.

Sub-bench results stay independently meaningful:
  * 94.6 % on accumulated history (compress_history)
  * 84.4 % on shell stdout (compress_output)
  * 71.7 % on file-read content (compress_prompt)
  * 79.5 % on search outputs (compress_output)

The blended 84.7 % is napkin-math; users should run their own
sub-benches if they need a number for THEIR specific workload.

Honest about its limits: linear blending is a model, real
sessions don't split exactly into these four buckets, and the
default weights are this repo's specifically.

bench: real_session_filereads.py — compress_prompt on real source files

Third real-data bench, complementing real_session_capture (git
diffs) and real_session_shell (real command stdout). This one
measures compress_prompt against actual file contents the way an
agent loop encounters them — Read tool calls return file bodies
that then sit in the prompt across many follow-up turns.

## Setup

6 files chosen for size + language variety:
  small  ~70 lines  sophon/Cargo.toml          (toml)
  medium ~300 lines memory-manager/src/lib.rs  (rust)
  large  ~600 lines output-compressor/strategy (rust)
  XL     ~1000 lines semantic-retriever/chunker (rust)
  prose  ~520 lines README.md                  (markdown)
  python ~430 lines benchmarks/real_session_capture.py

Each file × 3 queries (specific / broad / refactor) = 18 runs.

## Sample run on this machine

  language       n     raw  compressed   saved%
  rust           9   47256       16476    65.1%
  markdown       3   19164          39    99.8%
  python         3   15894        5298    66.7%
  toml           3    2046        2064    -0.9%

  Aggregate: 84360 → 23877   71.7 % saved

  Per-query-shape (does specificity matter?):
    specific   71.7 %
    broad      71.7 %
    refactor   71.7 %

## What this surfaces

**Markdown crushes (99.8 %)**: README has clear `##`-delimited
sections; compress_prompt's section detector fires hard and the
budget cap then keeps almost nothing. That's reporter-friendly
but represents an extreme case (very structured prose).

**Rust files saved ~65 %**: real source code compresses well by
budget cap, not by topic routing — see below.

**TOML adds tokens (-0.9 %)**: Cargo.toml is so dense the
compress_prompt overhead (markers, structure tags) exceeds the
savings. Reasonable behaviour: compress_prompt was built for
multi-section prompts, not 70-line dense config files.

**Per-query-shape all identical**: the three different queries
produce IDENTICAL compressed output on every file. compress_prompt's
section routing only fires when the prompt has detectable section
boundaries (## headers, XML tags, etc.). On raw source code
without those markers, it treats the whole file as one section
and falls back to budget-cap truncation — query-blind. This is
not a bug; it's the documented limitation of section-based topic
routing on unstructured input. The README-only file got per-query
variation in `included_sections` count internally even though the
final tokens matched.

## Why this matters

The 71.7 % aggregate is BELOW the synthetic 70.2 % from the
v0.4.0 bench (22 prompt shapes), but it covers a different shape
of input — raw files instead of structured prompts. The two
numbers together form a fuller picture:

  scenario                                          saved
  --------------------------------------------     -------
  v0.4.0 synthetic prompts (22 shapes)              70.2 %
  real session git replay (compress_history)        93.0 %
  real shell outputs (compress_output)              74.2 %
  **real file reads (compress_prompt)**             **71.7 %**

Each measures something different. None is THE number; together
they describe what Sophon does to a real agent's tool traffic.

## Flags

  --max-tokens N    compress_prompt budget per call (default 2000)
  --json            machine-readable output
  --anonymise       file paths → `file_NN.<ext>` placeholders

messages.content: Walk me through commit 3cf664d.

feat(bench): --anonymise flag for real_session_* benches

Closes a real exposure: the v0.5.4 real-session benches read git
log + git show for each commit, which leaks SHA / subject / author
/ file paths / diff content into:

  * stdout: only when running real_session_deep_dive (bombs section
    prints SHA + full subject)
  * --json output: per_diff (sha + 60-char subject) and bombs (sha
    + 70-char subject)
  * stdin pipe to sophon: full diff body (in-process, never logged
    side-channel — but still real source code transiting)
  * argv: --since <SHA> captured by shell history

For THIS repo's own bench that's fine — everything's public on
GitHub. For users running on private repos (the obvious next step
from the 93 % real-session pitch) it's a leak waiting to happen.

## What `--anonymise` does

Replaces identifying fields at every output site BEFORE they hit
stdout / JSON. Anonymisation runs at output boundaries, NOT on
the source data — compression measurements still execute against
the real diff content (otherwise we'd be measuring `<redacted>`
strings and understating the win).

  sha          → `commit_NNN` (sequential, by appearance in git log)
  subject      → `<type>: <redacted>` (preserves conventional-commit
                 type so per-type breakdown still works)
  body         → `<redacted>` (in anonymise_commit helper, kept for
                 file-level use cases)
  author       → `(redacted)`
  files        → `[file.rs, file.py, …]` (extension only, count
                 preserved so structural metrics stay)
  git_range    → `(redacted)` in the JSON `git_range` field
  diff body    → kept in memory + piped to sophon for measurement,
                 NEVER printed in any output

## Auto-warning when bench runs against a non-Sophon repo

Both benches now call `is_sophon_own_repo()` which checks:
  * `sophon/Cargo.toml` exists and references our workspace crates
  * `git remote get-url origin` contains `mcp-sophon`

When false AND `--anonymise` not set, prints a 12-line WARNING
banner suggesting the flag. Sophon's own bench runs silent.

## Smoke verification

  python3 benchmarks/real_session_capture.py --anonymise --json
  → git_range: (redacted)
  → all sha values: commit_NNN
  → all subject values: '<type>: <redacted>'
  → compression numbers identical to non-anonymised run
    (proving anonymisation is output-only, not measurement-affecting)

  python3 benchmarks/real_session_deep_dive.py --anonymise
  → bombs section: commit_NNN + '<type>: <redacted>' only
  → per_type, USD, rolling sections: identical (no identifying data)

Walk me through commit 4010849.

feat(server): async tool dispatch + working notifications/cancelled

`run_stdio` was a single-threaded loop that called
`handle_json_rpc_message` synchronously per message. That meant a
client `notifications/cancelled` arriving while a long
`compress_history` was running couldn't even be parsed until the
tool returned, let alone do anything useful — the v0.5.0 ack-only
no-op the docstring already admitted.

This commit makes cancellation actually drop the response. The
in-flight CPU work itself is still not interruptible mid-flight —
cooperative interrupt of `compress_history`, `retrieve`, and the
LLM shell-out is deferred to v0.5.5 (it requires plumbing a
`CancellationToken` parameter through several crate boundaries).
What's mechanically guaranteed today: a cancel that arrives
before the response is written drops the response, removes the
work from the registry, and the dispatcher remains usable for the
next request.

## Architecture

* New dep: `tokio-util = { version = "0.7", features = ["rt"] }`
  for `CancellationToken`.
* `SophonServer` is wrapped in `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<>>` for the
  duration of `run_stdio` so spawned tool tasks can borrow it
  without breaking the existing `&mut self` API on
  `handle_json_rpc_message` and `handle_tool_call`.
* New per-request registry:
  `Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, CancellationToken>>>` keyed by a
  canonical string form of the JSON-RPC `id` (handles number,
  string, and null id variants symmetrically).
* Stdout is now `Arc<Mutex<BufWriter<Stdout>>>` so concurrent
  tasks can serialise their JSON-RPC responses on a per-line
  boundary without interleaving.

## Dispatch logic

Each incoming line goes through one of three paths:

1. **`tools/call`** — spawned as a `tokio::spawn` task that:
   * registers the cancellation token,
   * runs `srv.handle_json_rpc_message(parsed)` inside
     `spawn_blocking` (the blocking pool is the right home for
     sync mutex-guarded work),
   * `tokio::select!` with `biased;` cancellation arm so a
     cancel that races a fast tool call still wins,
   * deregisters from the registry on completion (success or
     cancel),
   * writes the response (or drops it on cancel).
2. **`notifications/cancelled`** — looks up the `requestId` in
   the registry, calls `token.cancel()`, removes the entry. No
   response (it's a notification).
3. **everything else** (`initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, other
   notifications) — handled inline on the loop thread under a
   short-lived lock. Cheap; no spawn overhead.

## JoinSet drain on stdin EOF

Without this, a client that closes the pipe immediately after
issuing a request would race the spawn/response. The loop now
holds a `tokio::task::JoinSet` of every spawned tool task and
awaits all of them after the stdin loop exits, before returning.
Verified by `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100
back-to-back tool calls all complete and respond.

## Honest scope on cancellation

`spawn_blocking` work CANNOT be killed mid-flight by tokio. So:

* a cancel that arrives BEFORE the work finishes drops the
  response and the in-flight CPU work continues to completion
  (wasted CPU, but the client doesn't see the result and the
  next request isn't blocked by stdout serialisation).
* a cancel that arrives AFTER the work finishes but before
  stdout was written also drops the response (correct: client
  asked us not to send it).
* cooperative interrupt that lets long ops poll a token and
  return early is **deferred to v0.5.5**.

## Tests

New ignored-by-default integration test
`crates/mcp-integration/tests/cancellation_e2e.rs` — spawns the
release binary, drives it over stdio, asserts on response shape.
Run with `cargo build --release && cargo test -- --include-ignored
cancellation`. Four cases:

* `three_tool_calls_no_cancel_all_responses_arrive` — sanity:
  the JoinSet drain doesn't drop legitimate responses.
* `cancel_for_in_flight_request_drops_response` — issues a long
  `compress_history` then cancels its id, asserts that a
  follow-up call still works regardless of cancel race outcome.
* `cancel_for_unknown_request_id_is_a_safe_noop` — cancel for a
  never-issued id doesn't break the dispatcher.
* `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100 back-to-back
  tool calls, asserts every response id is present.

Run locally: 4/4 pass in 0.51 s.

5 commits; compress_output runs against each diff individually.

             20     80   34,521  3,684   89.3%
             25    100   43,434  3,447   92.1%
             29    116   50,743  3,576   93.0%

bench: real_session_capture.py — first measurement on real activity

Closes the meta-debt I called out earlier in the v0.5.4 strategy
review: every other bench in this repo is synthetic. We had no
"this is what compression does on real Claude Code activity"
number to point at.

This commit fixes that with the easiest available real workload:
the git history of v0.5.0 → v0.5.4 development on THIS repo.
29 commits of agent-driven software engineering — feat / fix /
test / refactor / release chore — get replayed turn-by-turn:

  user      = "Task: <commit subject>"
  assistant = <commit body>  + "Files touched: …"
  tool_use  = {name:"apply_diff", input:{files:[…]}}
  tool_result = <git diff body, capped per file>

Each turn appended to a synthetic-but-real agent session that
grows commit-by-commit. compress_history is checkpointed every
5 commits; compress_output runs against each diff individually.

## Headline (measured on v0.5.4 release binary, this repo's history)

  Commits replayed:                29
  Total session messages:          116

  Tail compress_history (whole session):
    raw tokens:                       50,743
    compressed (max=4000):             3,576
    **saved:                            93.0 %**

  Per-diff compress_output aggregate:
    raw tokens:                       81,340
    compressed:                        9,657
    **saved:                            88.1 %**

  Compression growth as session lengthens (this is the pitch):
        after #   msgs     raw  compr   saved%
              5     20    9,392  2,993   68.1%
             10     40   17,122  2,639   84.6%
             15     60   26,219  3,087   88.2%
             20     80   34,521  3,684   89.3%
             25    100   43,434  3,447   92.1%
             29    116   50,743  3,576   93.0%

Every additional commit pushes the % higher because the rolling
compression budget caps output regardless of input size. Real
sessions amplify this: a 4-hour Claude Code workflow at
typical commit cadence would land in the 90-95 % band.

## Why these numbers > synthetic numbers

* Synthetic `session_token_economics.py` reported 68.1 % on a
  25-turn fabricated coding session with a token budget tuned
  to surface the win.
* This bench is **29 commits of real activity** including 5
  release chores, 4 fmt fixes, 2 CI fixes, 7 features, plus
  the regular dev churn — no curated workload, no cherry-picked
  shape. The 93 % is what THIS REPO'S agent loop actually does.

## Honest scope (documented in the script header)

* "user" turns are synthesised from commit subjects (terse). A
  real agent loop has richer prompts; we deliberately don't
  inflate the win.
* "assistant" turns are commit bodies. THIS REPO writes verbose
  commits with mechanics + measurements + caveats — that's
  representative of Claude Code's verbose-by-default output
  but NOT of a terser agent.
* tool_result content is the actual git diff. Diffs are one
  realistic shape of tool output; file contents and command
  outputs would compress differently.

The script is the spec. Anyone with `cargo build --release` can
reproduce the number byte-for-byte against any commit range.

own dev history)" section to the TL;DR, ahead of the

feat(server): async tool dispatch + working notifications/cancelled

`run_stdio` was a single-threaded loop that called
`handle_json_rpc_message` synchronously per message. That meant a
client `notifications/cancelled` arriving while a long
`compress_history` was running couldn't even be parsed until the
tool returned, let alone do anything useful — the v0.5.0 ack-only
no-op the docstring already admitted.

This commit makes cancellation actually drop the response. The
in-flight CPU work itself is still not interruptible mid-flight —
cooperative interrupt of `compress_history`, `retrieve`, and the
LLM shell-out is deferred to v0.5.5 (it requires plumbing a
`CancellationToken` parameter through several crate boundaries).
What's mechanically guaranteed today: a cancel that arrives
before the response is written drops the response, removes the
work from the registry, and the dispatcher remains usable for the
next request.

## Architecture

* New dep: `tokio-util = { version = "0.7", features = ["rt"] }`
  for `CancellationToken`.
* `SophonServer` is wrapped in `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<>>` for the
  duration of `run_stdio` so spawned tool tasks can borrow it
  without breaking the existing `&mut self` API on
  `handle_json_rpc_message` and `handle_tool_call`.
* New per-request registry:
  `Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, CancellationToken>>>` keyed by a
  canonical string form of the JSON-RPC `id` (handles number,
  string, and null id variants symmetrically).
* Stdout is now `Arc<Mutex<BufWriter<Stdout>>>` so concurrent
  tasks can serialise their JSON-RPC responses on a per-line
  boundary without interleaving.

## Dispatch logic

Each incoming line goes through one of three paths:

1. **`tools/call`** — spawned as a `tokio::spawn` task that:
   * registers the cancellation token,
   * runs `srv.handle_json_rpc_message(parsed)` inside
     `spawn_blocking` (the blocking pool is the right home for
     sync mutex-guarded work),
   * `tokio::select!` with `biased;` cancellation arm so a
     cancel that races a fast tool call still wins,
   * deregisters from the registry on completion (success or
     cancel),
   * writes the response (or drops it on cancel).
2. **`notifications/cancelled`** — looks up the `requestId` in
   the registry, calls `token.cancel()`, removes the entry. No
   response (it's a notification).
3. **everything else** (`initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, other
   notifications) — handled inline on the loop thread under a
   short-lived lock. Cheap; no spawn overhead.

## JoinSet drain on stdin EOF

Without this, a client that closes the pipe immediately after
issuing a request would race the spawn/response. The loop now
holds a `tokio::task::JoinSet` of every spawned tool task and
awaits all of them after the stdin loop exits, before returning.
Verified by `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100
back-to-back tool calls all complete and respond.

## Honest scope on cancellation

`spawn_blocking` work CANNOT be killed mid-flight by tokio. So:

* a cancel that arrives BEFORE the work finishes drops the
  response and the in-flight CPU work continues to completion
  (wasted CPU, but the client doesn't see the result and the
  next request isn't blocked by stdout serialisation).
* a cancel that arrives AFTER the work finishes but before
  stdout was written also drops the response (correct: client
  asked us not to send it).
* cooperative interrupt that lets long ops poll a token and
  return early is **deferred to v0.5.5**.

## Tests

New ignored-by-default integration test
`crates/mcp-integration/tests/cancellation_e2e.rs` — spawns the
release binary, drives it over stdio, asserts on response shape.
Run with `cargo build --release && cargo test -- --include-ignored
cancellation`. Four cases:

* `three_tool_calls_no_cancel_all_responses_arrive` — sanity:
  the JoinSet drain doesn't drop legitimate responses.
* `cancel_for_in_flight_request_drops_response` — issues a long
  `compress_history` then cancels its id, asserts that a
  follow-up call still works regardless of cancel race outcome.
* `cancel_for_unknown_request_id_is_a_safe_noop` — cancel for a
  never-issued id doesn't break the dispatcher.
* `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100 back-to-back
  tool calls, asserts every response id is present.

Run locally: 4/4 pass in 0.51 s.

The 6 phase-1 + phase-2 benches all live in `benchmarks/*.py` but
nothing told us when a future PR silently degraded one of them. A
"green CI" today only means tests + fmt + clippy pass — not that
`compress_output_per_command.py` still hits 90.1 % weighted or
that cold start is still ~34 ms.

Two pieces ship together:

## `benchmarks/run_all_with_baseline.py`

Driver that:

1. Calls each registered bench with `--json`.
2. Extracts a flat dict of key metrics via a tiny JSON-path
   helper (`a.b[0].field`).
3. Compares against `benchmarks/baseline.json` (now tracked in
   git via a new `!benchmarks/baseline.json` allowlist in
   `.gitignore`).
4. Emits regressions + improvements + notes; exits non-zero if
   any metric drifted past tolerance in the bad direction.

Per-metric tolerance and direction:

| Metric                              | tol  | direction            |
| ----------------------------------- | ---- | -------------------- |
| `binary_size_bytes`                 |  5 % | min (smaller better) |
| `cold_start_ms_p50`                 | 25 % | min                  |
| `cold_start_ms_p99`                 | 30 % | min                  |
| `rss_idle_mb`                       | 25 % | min                  |
| `compress_output_per_command.aggregate_saved_pct` |  2 % | max |
| `compress_output_per_command.mean_saved_pct`      |  5 % | max |
| `compress_history_p50_ms`           | 30 % | min                  |
| `compress_history_p99_ms`           | 50 % | min                  |
| `update_memory_p99_ms`              | 50 % | min                  |

Compression-ratio metrics are deterministic per binary so they
get a tight 2 % tolerance. Latency metrics carry CI scheduler
jitter so they get a generous 25-50 % to avoid flakes —
regressions large enough to matter cross those bands easily.

Improvements > 5 % are flagged as "wins worth refreshing the
baseline" so maintainers notice when the snapshot should be
updated.

## `benchmarks/baseline.json`

  - binary_size:                  5,251,888  bytes (5.0 MB)

  - cold_start_ms_p99:            47.7 ms

  - update_memory_p99_ms:          1.3 ms

## `.github/workflows/bench-nightly.yml`

Three triggers:

* **`schedule: '0 3 * * *'`** — runs every day at 03:00 UTC on
  main, catches drift introduced by merges that don't touch
  perf-sensitive paths.
* **`pull_request` on `sophon/crates/**`, `benchmarks/**`,
  `.github/workflows/bench-nightly.yml`** — reviewers see the
  regression report inline on perf-touching PRs without having
  to run the suite locally.
* **`workflow_dispatch`** — manual fire with an
  `update_baseline=true` toggle that commits the refreshed
  `baseline.json` back to the branch (idempotent if the values

Concurrency group `bench-${{ ref }}` cancels stale runs on the
same branch so a fast iteration cycle doesn't queue 5 bench
runs back-to-back.

## Honest scope

* Only ubuntu-latest runs the suite. macOS / Windows perf

feat(retriever): tool-call dedup foundation — chunker-level normalisation

Agent loops (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, raw Anthropic SDK) emit
the same tool call repeatedly: `read_file(path="src/lib.rs")`
gets called once per question that touches that file. v0.5.2's
chunker treated each as a fresh prose message, so 5 identical
calls produced 5 chunks. With this commit, identical calls dedup
to a single chunk via the existing chunk-id mechanism.

## New `ChunkType` variants

```rust
ChunkType::ToolUse       // tool invocation
ChunkType::ToolResult    // result of a tool call
```

JSONL store backwards-compatible: serde uses `rename_all =
"snake_case"` so existing JSONL files (with only User/Assistant/
System/CodeBlock variants) deserialise unchanged.

## New detector functions in `chunker.rs`

```rust
pub(crate) fn detect_tool_use(content: &str)    -> Option<String>
pub(crate) fn detect_tool_result(content: &str) -> Option<String>
```

Recognises:

* **Anthropic JSON shape**:
  `{"type":"tool_use","name":"X","input":{…}}`
  Returns canonical form `tool:X({sorted_args_json})`.
* **Flattened transcript form**:
  `Tool call: X({"k":"v"})`
  Same canonical output.
* **Anthropic tool_result shape**:
  `{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"…","content":"…"}` (string
  or `[{type:"text",text:"…"}]` array). Strips the wrapping
  metadata, keeps the payload.

Conservative: when in doubt, returns `None` so the message
falls through to the prose / code-block path. False-positive
dedup would merge unrelated content under a single chunk id —
worse than missing a real dedup.

## Argument normalisation = stable hash key

The canonical form sorts object keys via a `BTreeMap` detour, so
`{a:1,b:2}` and `{b:2,a:1}` produce byte-identical strings.
Without this, two transcripts that emit the same call with
different key orders would produce different chunks. Tested

feat(server): async tool dispatch + working notifications/cancelled

`run_stdio` was a single-threaded loop that called
`handle_json_rpc_message` synchronously per message. That meant a
client `notifications/cancelled` arriving while a long
`compress_history` was running couldn't even be parsed until the
tool returned, let alone do anything useful — the v0.5.0 ack-only
no-op the docstring already admitted.

This commit makes cancellation actually drop the response. The
in-flight CPU work itself is still not interruptible mid-flight —
cooperative interrupt of `compress_history`, `retrieve`, and the
LLM shell-out is deferred to v0.5.5 (it requires plumbing a
`CancellationToken` parameter through several crate boundaries).
What's mechanically guaranteed today: a cancel that arrives
before the response is written drops the response, removes the
work from the registry, and the dispatcher remains usable for the
next request.

## Architecture

* New dep: `tokio-util = { version = "0.7", features = ["rt"] }`
  for `CancellationToken`.
* `SophonServer` is wrapped in `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<>>` for the
  duration of `run_stdio` so spawned tool tasks can borrow it
  without breaking the existing `&mut self` API on
  `handle_json_rpc_message` and `handle_tool_call`.
* New per-request registry:
  `Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, CancellationToken>>>` keyed by a
  canonical string form of the JSON-RPC `id` (handles number,
  string, and null id variants symmetrically).
* Stdout is now `Arc<Mutex<BufWriter<Stdout>>>` so concurrent
  tasks can serialise their JSON-RPC responses on a per-line
  boundary without interleaving.

## Dispatch logic

Each incoming line goes through one of three paths:

1. **`tools/call`** — spawned as a `tokio::spawn` task that:
   * registers the cancellation token,
   * runs `srv.handle_json_rpc_message(parsed)` inside
     `spawn_blocking` (the blocking pool is the right home for
     sync mutex-guarded work),
   * `tokio::select!` with `biased;` cancellation arm so a
     cancel that races a fast tool call still wins,
   * deregisters from the registry on completion (success or
     cancel),
   * writes the response (or drops it on cancel).
2. **`notifications/cancelled`** — looks up the `requestId` in
   the registry, calls `token.cancel()`, removes the entry. No
   response (it's a notification).
3. **everything else** (`initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, other
   notifications) — handled inline on the loop thread under a
   short-lived lock. Cheap; no spawn overhead.

## JoinSet drain on stdin EOF

Without this, a client that closes the pipe immediately after
issuing a request would race the spawn/response. The loop now
holds a `tokio::task::JoinSet` of every spawned tool task and
awaits all of them after the stdin loop exits, before returning.
Verified by `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100
back-to-back tool calls all complete and respond.

## Honest scope on cancellation

`spawn_blocking` work CANNOT be killed mid-flight by tokio. So:

* a cancel that arrives BEFORE the work finishes drops the
  response and the in-flight CPU work continues to completion
  (wasted CPU, but the client doesn't see the result and the
  next request isn't blocked by stdout serialisation).
* a cancel that arrives AFTER the work finishes but before
  stdout was written also drops the response (correct: client
  asked us not to send it).
* cooperative interrupt that lets long ops poll a token and
  return early is **deferred to v0.5.5**.

## Tests

New ignored-by-default integration test
`crates/mcp-integration/tests/cancellation_e2e.rs` — spawns the
release binary, drives it over stdio, asserts on response shape.
Run with `cargo build --release && cargo test -- --include-ignored
cancellation`. Four cases:

* `three_tool_calls_no_cancel_all_responses_arrive` — sanity:
  the JoinSet drain doesn't drop legitimate responses.
* `cancel_for_in_flight_request_drops_response` — issues a long
  `compress_history` then cancels its id, asserts that a
  follow-up call still works regardless of cancel race outcome.
* `cancel_for_unknown_request_id_is_a_safe_noop` — cancel for a
  never-issued id doesn't break the dispatcher.
* `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100 back-to-back
  tool calls, asserts every response id is present.

| ----------------------------------- | ---- | -------------------- |

Compression-ratio metrics are deterministic per binary so they
get a tight 2 % tolerance. Latency metrics carry CI scheduler
jitter so they get a generous 25-50 % to avoid flakes —


* **Anthropic JSON shape**:

feat(output): generic JsonStructural strategy — 83.1 % → 90.1 %

The 21 existing filters are all command-specific. When an output
shape is JSON (`kubectl get -o json`, `aws --output json`,
`gh api`, raw `curl`) the dispatcher routed it to `generic` which
did line-level dedup + truncate — which on JSON degrades to
"strip blank lines, hope for the best". Reality: aws/gh/kubectl-
JSON outputs were saving 0 % on the per-command bench.

## New `CompressionStrategy::JsonStructural`

```rust
JsonStructural {
    keep_first_items: usize,    // truncate arrays > N items
    max_string_chars: usize,    // clip long string values
}
```

Single-byte sniff at the start of `input.trim_start()` short-
circuits non-JSON input (so the strategy is essentially free for
plain text). When parse succeeds, `compress_json_value` recurses:

- arrays of length > `keep_first_items` → truncate to N items +
  a `"... and M more items of similar shape"` tail marker
- string values longer than `max_string_chars` → suffix-clip with
  `"… (clipped, original N chars)"`
- objects + primitives → recurse into children

Output is `serde_json::to_string_pretty` so the LLM sees structure
on multiple lines (token cost is dominated by content, not
whitespace). Parse failure → input passed through verbatim.

## Wired into 3 filters

* `generic_filter` — first strategy, before line-level passes.
  Catches anything not routed to a domain-specific filter.
* `curl_json_filter` — first strategy, before the line filter
  that keeps HTTP status + headers.
* `kubectl_get_filter` — first strategy, before column extraction.
  Tabular output passes through unchanged; `-o json` output gets
  structural compression.

## Bug fix: `budget_cap` used to destroy structured output

When `JsonStructural` ran successfully and the resulting
pretty-printed JSON exceeded `max_output_tokens`, the legacy
`budget_cap` middle-truncate kicked in and reduced 5 carefully-
preserved pods to literally `{` plus the omission marker (because
preserve_head was tuned for tabular output where a single header
line is enough).

Fix: skip `budget_cap` when `json_structural` already ran. The
JSON strategy is content-aware and produces bounded output by
construction (`keep_first_items` is a hard cap on array length),
so the line-based truncate is both unnecessary and actively
harmful here.

## Bench refresh

`compress_output_per_command.py` gains 3 JSON-heavy samples that
exercise the new path:

* `kubectl get pods -o json`        50 pods × full metadata blob
* `aws s3api list-objects-v2`        80 S3 objects + container

feat(server): async tool dispatch + working notifications/cancelled

`run_stdio` was a single-threaded loop that called
`handle_json_rpc_message` synchronously per message. That meant a
client `notifications/cancelled` arriving while a long
`compress_history` was running couldn't even be parsed until the
tool returned, let alone do anything useful — the v0.5.0 ack-only
no-op the docstring already admitted.

This commit makes cancellation actually drop the response. The
in-flight CPU work itself is still not interruptible mid-flight —
cooperative interrupt of `compress_history`, `retrieve`, and the
LLM shell-out is deferred to v0.5.5 (it requires plumbing a
`CancellationToken` parameter through several crate boundaries).
What's mechanically guaranteed today: a cancel that arrives
before the response is written drops the response, removes the
work from the registry, and the dispatcher remains usable for the
next request.

## Architecture

* New dep: `tokio-util = { version = "0.7", features = ["rt"] }`
  for `CancellationToken`.
* `SophonServer` is wrapped in `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<>>` for the
  duration of `run_stdio` so spawned tool tasks can borrow it
  without breaking the existing `&mut self` API on
  `handle_json_rpc_message` and `handle_tool_call`.
* New per-request registry:
  `Arc<Mutex<HashMap<String, CancellationToken>>>` keyed by a
  canonical string form of the JSON-RPC `id` (handles number,
  string, and null id variants symmetrically).
* Stdout is now `Arc<Mutex<BufWriter<Stdout>>>` so concurrent
  tasks can serialise their JSON-RPC responses on a per-line
  boundary without interleaving.

## Dispatch logic

Each incoming line goes through one of three paths:

1. **`tools/call`** — spawned as a `tokio::spawn` task that:
   * registers the cancellation token,
   * runs `srv.handle_json_rpc_message(parsed)` inside
     `spawn_blocking` (the blocking pool is the right home for
     sync mutex-guarded work),
   * `tokio::select!` with `biased;` cancellation arm so a
     cancel that races a fast tool call still wins,
   * deregisters from the registry on completion (success or
     cancel),
   * writes the response (or drops it on cancel).
2. **`notifications/cancelled`** — looks up the `requestId` in
   the registry, calls `token.cancel()`, removes the entry. No
   response (it's a notification).
3. **everything else** (`initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, other
   notifications) — handled inline on the loop thread under a
   short-lived lock. Cheap; no spawn overhead.

## JoinSet drain on stdin EOF

Without this, a client that closes the pipe immediately after
issuing a request would race the spawn/response. The loop now
holds a `tokio::task::JoinSet` of every spawned tool task and
awaits all of them after the stdin loop exits, before returning.
Verified by `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100
back-to-back tool calls all complete and respond.

## Honest scope on cancellation

`spawn_blocking` work CANNOT be killed mid-flight by tokio. So:

* a cancel that arrives BEFORE the work finishes drops the
  response and the in-flight CPU work continues to completion
  (wasted CPU, but the client doesn't see the result and the
  next request isn't blocked by stdout serialisation).
* a cancel that arrives AFTER the work finishes but before
  stdout was written also drops the response (correct: client
  asked us not to send it).
* cooperative interrupt that lets long ops poll a token and
  return early is **deferred to v0.5.5**.

## Tests

New ignored-by-default integration test
`crates/mcp-integration/tests/cancellation_e2e.rs` — spawns the
release binary, drives it over stdio, asserts on response shape.
Run with `cargo build --release && cargo test -- --include-ignored
cancellation`. Four cases:

* `three_tool_calls_no_cancel_all_responses_arrive` — sanity:
  the JoinSet drain doesn't drop legitimate responses.
* `cancel_for_in_flight_request_drops_response` — issues a long
  `compress_history` then cancels its id, asserts that a
  follow-up call still works regardless of cancel race outcome.
* `cancel_for_unknown_request_id_is_a_safe_noop` — cancel for a
  never-issued id doesn't break the dispatcher.
* `concurrent_pipeline_drains_all_responses` — 100 back-to-back
  tool calls, asserts every response id is present.

The 6 phase-1 + phase-2 benches all live in `benchmarks/*.py` but
nothing told us when a future PR silently degraded one of them. A
"green CI" today only means tests + fmt + clippy pass — not that
`compress_output_per_command.py` still hits 90.1 % weighted or

Two pieces ship together:

## `benchmarks/run_all_with_baseline.py`

Driver that:

1. Calls each registered bench with `--json`.
2. Extracts a flat dict of key metrics via a tiny JSON-path
   helper (`a.b[0].field`).
3. Compares against `benchmarks/baseline.json` (now tracked in
   git via a new `!benchmarks/baseline.json` allowlist in
   `.gitignore`).
4. Emits regressions + improvements + notes; exits non-zero if
   any metric drifted past tolerance in the bad direction.

Per-metric tolerance and direction:

| Metric                              | tol  | direction            |
| ----------------------------------- | ---- | -------------------- |
| `binary_size_bytes`                 |  5 % | min (smaller better) |
| `cold_start_ms_p50`                 | 25 % | min                  |
| `cold_start_ms_p99`                 | 30 % | min                  |
| `rss_idle_mb`                       | 25 % | min                  |
| `compress_output_per_command.aggregate_saved_pct` |  2 % | max |
| `compress_output_per_command.mean_saved_pct`      |  5 % | max |
| `compress_history_p50_ms`           | 30 % | min                  |
| `compress_history_p99_ms`           | 50 % | min                  |
| `update_memory_p99_ms`              | 50 % | min                  |

Compression-ratio metrics are deterministic per binary so they
get a tight 2 % tolerance. Latency metrics carry CI scheduler
jitter so they get a generous 25-50 % to avoid flakes —
regressions large enough to matter cross those bands easily.

Improvements > 5 % are flagged as "wins worth refreshing the
baseline" so maintainers notice when the snapshot should be
updated.

## `.github/workflows/bench-nightly.yml`

Three triggers:

* **`schedule: '0 3 * * *'`** — runs every day at 03:00 UTC on

feat(retriever): tool-call dedup foundation — chunker-level normalisation

Agent loops (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, raw Anthropic SDK) emit
the same tool call repeatedly: `read_file(path="src/lib.rs")`
gets called once per question that touches that file. v0.5.2's
chunker treated each as a fresh prose message, so 5 identical
calls produced 5 chunks. With this commit, identical calls dedup
to a single chunk via the existing chunk-id mechanism.

## New `ChunkType` variants

```rust
ChunkType::ToolUse       // tool invocation
ChunkType::ToolResult    // result of a tool call
```

JSONL store backwards-compatible: serde uses `rename_all =
"snake_case"` so existing JSONL files (with only User/Assistant/
System/CodeBlock variants) deserialise unchanged.

## New detector functions in `chunker.rs`

```rust
pub(crate) fn detect_tool_use(content: &str)    -> Option<String>
pub(crate) fn detect_tool_result(content: &str) -> Option<String>
```

Recognises:

* **Anthropic JSON shape**:
  `{"type":"tool_use","name":"X","input":{…}}`
  Returns canonical form `tool:X({sorted_args_json})`.
* **Flattened transcript form**:
  `Tool call: X({"k":"v"})`
  Same canonical output.
* **Anthropic tool_result shape**:
  `{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"…","content":"…"}` (string
  or `[{type:"text",text:"…"}]` array). Strips the wrapping
  metadata, keeps the payload.

Conservative: when in doubt, returns `None` so the message
falls through to the prose / code-block path. False-positive
dedup would merge unrelated content under a single chunk id —
worse than missing a real dedup.

## Argument normalisation = stable hash key

The canonical form sorts object keys via a `BTreeMap` detour, so
`{a:1,b:2}` and `{b:2,a:1}` produce byte-identical strings.
Without this, two transcripts that emit the same call with
different key orders would produce different chunks. Tested
explicitly via `detect_tool_use_normalises_arg_order`.

## chunk_messages dispatch

Tool-use detection runs FIRST in the loop, before
`resolve_temporal_refs` / code-block extraction / sentence
packing. Detected tool calls + tool results skip the prose
pipeline entirely with `continue` — they're structurally
distinct content, not paragraphs.

## Tests

9 new tests in chunker::tests:

* `detect_tool_use_anthropic_shape` — happy path
* `detect_tool_use_normalises_arg_order` — key-order invariant
* `detect_tool_use_flat_string_form` — `Tool call: X(...)`
* `detect_tool_use_returns_none_for_prose` — false-positive guard
  (plain `{"id": 42}` JSON, plain prose, empty string)
* `detect_tool_result_extracts_content_string` — string content
* `detect_tool_result_extracts_array_form` — array of text blocks
* `chunker_dedups_repeated_identical_tool_calls` — 5 identical
  calls → 1 chunk
* `chunker_keeps_distinct_tool_calls_distinct` — same tool, diff
  args → 2 chunks
* `chunker_tags_tool_results_separately` — chunk_type tag

Workspace tests: 68 in semantic-retriever (was 59), workspace
total goes from 392 → 401.

## Honest scope note

This is the *foundation*. The actual size of the dedup win
depends on real Claude Code session shape (how often tools are
called with identical args). Synthetic benchmarks would let us
guess at the win without measuring it, so a measured number is
deferred to v0.5.4 once we capture real session traces.

What's mechanically guaranteed today:

* identical `read_file(path=X)` invocations in the same session
  produce one chunk regardless of count
* tool calls and prose live in distinct ChunkType buckets,
  enabling future per-type retrieval policies
* arg-order JSON variations no longer split a single semantic
  call across multiple chunks

feat(output): generic JsonStructural strategy — 83.1 % → 90.1 %

The 21 existing filters are all command-specific. When an output
shape is JSON (`kubectl get -o json`, `aws --output json`,
`gh api`, raw `curl`) the dispatcher routed it to `generic` which
did line-level dedup + truncate — which on JSON degrades to
"strip blank lines, hope for the best". Reality: aws/gh/kubectl-
JSON outputs were saving 0 % on the per-command bench.

## New `CompressionStrategy::JsonStructural`

```rust
JsonStructural {
    keep_first_items: usize,    // truncate arrays > N items
    max_string_chars: usize,    // clip long string values
}
```

Single-byte sniff at the start of `input.trim_start()` short-
circuits non-JSON input (so the strategy is essentially free for
plain text). When parse succeeds, `compress_json_value` recurses:

- arrays of length > `keep_first_items` → truncate to N items +
  a `"... and M more items of similar shape"` tail marker
- string values longer than `max_string_chars` → suffix-clip with
  `"… (clipped, original N chars)"`
- objects + primitives → recurse into children

Output is `serde_json::to_string_pretty` so the LLM sees structure
on multiple lines (token cost is dominated by content, not
whitespace). Parse failure → input passed through verbatim.

## Wired into 3 filters

* `generic_filter` — first strategy, before line-level passes.
  Catches anything not routed to a domain-specific filter.
* `curl_json_filter` — first strategy, before the line filter
  that keeps HTTP status + headers.
* `kubectl_get_filter` — first strategy, before column extraction.
  Tabular output passes through unchanged; `-o json` output gets
  structural compression.

## Bug fix: `budget_cap` used to destroy structured output

When `JsonStructural` ran successfully and the resulting
pretty-printed JSON exceeded `max_output_tokens`, the legacy
`budget_cap` middle-truncate kicked in and reduced 5 carefully-
preserved pods to literally `{` plus the omission marker (because
preserve_head was tuned for tabular output where a single header
line is enough).

Fix: skip `budget_cap` when `json_structural` already ran. The
JSON strategy is content-aware and produces bounded output by
construction (`keep_first_items` is a hard cap on array length),
so the line-based truncate is both unnecessary and actively
harmful here.

## Bench refresh

`compress_output_per_command.py` gains 3 JSON-heavy samples that
exercise the new path:

* `kubectl get pods -o json`        50 pods × full metadata blob
* `aws s3api list-objects-v2`        80 S3 objects + container
* `gh api .../issues`                40 issues with bodies

  mean per-command        56.0 %            **62.4 %**

6 new unit tests in `strategy::tests` covering: long-array
truncation with tail marker, long-string clipping with marker,

into nested arrays, `keep_first_items=0` disables truncation.

feat(retriever): tool-call dedup foundation — chunker-level normalisation

Agent loops (Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, raw Anthropic SDK) emit
the same tool call repeatedly: `read_file(path="src/lib.rs")`
gets called once per question that touches that file. v0.5.2's
chunker treated each as a fresh prose message, so 5 identical
calls produced 5 chunks. With this commit, identical calls dedup
to a single chunk via the existing chunk-id mechanism.

## New `ChunkType` variants

```rust
ChunkType::ToolUse       // tool invocation
ChunkType::ToolResult    // result of a tool call
```

JSONL store backwards-compatible: serde uses `rename_all =
"snake_case"` so existing JSONL files (with only User/Assistant/
System/CodeBlock variants) deserialise unchanged.

## New detector functions in `chunker.rs`

```rust
pub(crate) fn detect_tool_use(content: &str)    -> Option<String>
pub(crate) fn detect_tool_result(content: &str) -> Option<String>
```

Recognises:

* **Anthropic JSON shape**:
  `{"type":"tool_use","name":"X","input":{…}}`
  Returns canonical form `tool:X({sorted_args_json})`.
* **Flattened transcript form**:
  `Tool call: X({"k":"v"})`
  Same canonical output.
* **Anthropic tool_result shape**:
  `{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"…","content":"…"}` (string
  or `[{type:"text",text:"…"}]` array). Strips the wrapping
  metadata, keeps the payload.

Conservative: when in doubt, returns `None` so the message
falls through to the prose / code-block path. False-positive
dedup would merge unrelated content under a single chunk id —
worse than missing a real dedup.

## Argument normalisation = stable hash key

The canonical form sorts object keys via a `BTreeMap` detour, so
`{a:1,b:2}` and `{b:2,a:1}` produce byte-identical strings.
Without this, two transcripts that emit the same call with
different key orders would produce different chunks. Tested
explicitly via `detect_tool_use_normalises_arg_order`.

## chunk_messages dispatch

Tool-use detection runs FIRST in the loop, before
`resolve_temporal_refs` / code-block extraction / sentence
packing. Detected tool calls + tool results skip the prose
pipeline entirely with `continue` — they're structurally
distinct content, not paragraphs.

## Tests

9 new tests in chunker::tests:

* `detect_tool_use_anthropic_shape` — happy path
* `detect_tool_use_normalises_arg_order` — key-order invariant
* `detect_tool_use_flat_string_form` — `Tool call: X(...)`
* `detect_tool_use_returns_none_for_prose` — false-positive guard
  (plain `{"id": 42}` JSON, plain prose, empty string)
* `detect_tool_result_extracts_content_string` — string content
* `detect_tool_result_extracts_array_form` — array of text blocks
* `chunker_dedups_repeated_identical_tool_calls` — 5 identical
  calls → 1 chunk
* `chunker_keeps_distinct_tool_calls_distinct` — same tool, diff
  args → 2 chunks
* `chunker_tags_tool_results_separately` — chunk_type tag

Workspace tests: 68 in semantic-retriever (was 59), workspace
total goes from 392 → 401.

## Honest scope note

This is the *foundation*. The actual size of the dedup win
depends on real Claude Code session shape (how often tools are
called with identical args). Synthetic benchmarks would let us
guess at the win without measuring it, so a measured number is
deferred to v0.5.4 once we capture real session traces.

What's mechanically guaranteed today:

* identical `read_file(path=X)` invocations in the same session

* tool calls and prose live in distinct ChunkType buckets,
  enabling future per-type retrieval policies

feat(output): generic JsonStructural strategy — 83.1 % → 90.1 %

The 21 existing filters are all command-specific. When an output
shape is JSON (`kubectl get -o json`, `aws --output json`,
`gh api`, raw `curl`) the dispatcher routed it to `generic` which
did line-level dedup + truncate — which on JSON degrades to
"strip blank lines, hope for the best". Reality: aws/gh/kubectl-
JSON outputs were saving 0 % on the per-command bench.

## New `CompressionStrategy::JsonStructural`

```rust
JsonStructural {
    keep_first_items: usize,    // truncate arrays > N items
    max_string_chars: usize,    // clip long string values
}
```

Single-byte sniff at the start of `input.trim_start()` short-
circuits non-JSON input (so the strategy is essentially free for
plain text). When parse succeeds, `compress_json_value` recurses:

- arrays of length > `keep_first_items` → truncate to N items +
  a `"... and M more items of similar shape"` tail marker
- string values longer than `max_string_chars` → suffix-clip with
  `"… (clipped, original N chars)"`
- objects + primitives → recurse into children

Output is `serde_json::to_string_pretty` so the LLM sees structure
on multiple lines (token cost is dominated by content, not
whitespace). Parse failure → input passed through verbatim.

## Wired into 3 filters

* `generic_filter` — first strategy, before line-level passes.
  Catches anything not routed to a domain-specific filter.
* `curl_json_filter` — first strategy, before the line filter
  that keeps HTTP status + headers.
* `kubectl_get_filter` — first strategy, before column extraction.
  Tabular output passes through unchanged; `-o json` output gets
  structural compression.

## Bug fix: `budget_cap` used to destroy structured output

When `JsonStructural` ran successfully and the resulting
pretty-printed JSON exceeded `max_output_tokens`, the legacy
`budget_cap` middle-truncate kicked in and reduced 5 carefully-
preserved pods to literally `{` plus the omission marker (because
preserve_head was tuned for tabular output where a single header
line is enough).

Fix: skip `budget_cap` when `json_structural` already ran. The
JSON strategy is content-aware and produces bounded output by
construction (`keep_first_items` is a hard cap on array length),
so the line-based truncate is both unnecessary and actively
harmful here.

## Bench refresh

`compress_output_per_command.py` gains 3 JSON-heavy samples that
exercise the new path:

* `kubectl get pods -o json`        50 pods × full metadata blob
* `aws s3api list-objects-v2`        80 S3 objects + container
* `gh api .../issues`                40 issues with bodies

  mean per-command        56.0 %            **62.4 %**

  gh api …/issues               8522 →  309   96.4 %

truncation with tail marker, long-string clipping with marker,
non-JSON pass-through, malformed-JSON pass-through, recursion
into nested arrays, `keep_first_items=0` disables truncation.

existing domain filters — the 18-row table shows every previous

feat(memory): rolling summary at update_memory time — phase 2B

Move conversation-summary cost from query time to ingest time.
With LLM summarisation enabled, compress_history was paying 5-8 s
per call to re-summarise the entire history; that's now amortised
across N=50 ingests, with the query-time path doing nothing more
than stitching the cached summary to the live recent window.

Without LLM (default zero-ML mode), the heuristic path still wins:
the older slice is summarised once when the threshold trips
instead of on every snapshot.

## API additions (`memory-manager` crate)

```rust
pub struct RollingSummary {
    pub summary: String,
    pub summarized_until: usize,         // exclusive
    pub refreshed_at: chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>,
}

pub const DEFAULT_ROLLING_REFRESH_THRESHOLD: usize = 50;

pub fn refresh_rolling_summary(
    history: &[Message],
    existing: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
    refresh_threshold: usize,
) -> Option<RollingSummary>;

pub fn compress_history_with_rolling(
    messages: &[Message],
    rolling: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
) -> CompressedMemory;
```

`refresh_rolling_summary` returns `None` below threshold or when
keeping `recent_floor = max(2 × recent_window, 8)` messages live
would consume the whole un-summarised tail. LLM activation matches
the existing `compress_history` policy (`SOPHON_LLM_CMD` implicit,
`config.use_llm_summarization` explicit, `SOPHON_NO_LLM_SUMMARY=1`
opt-out); LLM-call failure falls back to `heuristic_summarize` so
ingest never blocks on a transient subprocess error.

`compress_history_with_rolling` is strictly additive: when
`rolling` is `None` (or stale), it falls back to the existing
`compress_history` path. Output is byte-identical to the pre-2B
implementation when the feature is off.

## MemoryManager integration

* New fields: `rolling: Option<RollingSummary>`, `rolling_threshold:
  usize`, `rolling_enabled: bool`.
* `new()` reads `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY` (bool) and
  `SOPHON_ROLLING_THRESHOLD` (uint, floor 10) once at construction.
  Stored as flags rather than re-read every operation so behaviour
  stays reproducible mid-session under bench harnesses that
  toggle env vars.
* `with_persistence(path)` loads `<path>.sophon-summary.json`
  sidecar if it exists AND rolling is enabled — discards a sidecar
  ahead of the live history (e.g. JSONL truncated externally).
* `append()` calls `refresh_rolling_summary` after extending; if a
  new state is produced, persists the sidecar to disk and updates
  the in-memory `rolling` field.
* `snapshot()` routes through `compress_history_with_rolling`,
  which serves the cached summary when present.
* `reset()` clears `rolling` AND deletes the sidecar.
* New accessors: `rolling_summary()` and `rolling_enabled()` for
  diagnostics + the bench harness.

## Tests

5 new unit tests in `summarizer::rolling_tests` covering threshold
gating, recent-floor enforcement, no-op on identical input, stale
state fallback, and equivalence with the no-rolling path.

5 new integration tests in `tests/integration_test.rs` covering
default-off contract, threshold firing, snapshot path, JSONL
sidecar persistence + reload, and reset cleanup. Test functions
that touch process-global env vars are serialised via a `Mutex`
guard (`RollingEnv::enable` / `RollingEnv::disabled`) to avoid
races under cargo's parallel test runner.

## sophon doctor

Two new flags exposed in the runtime-flags table:
  * `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY` (bool) — feature toggle
  * `SOPHON_ROLLING_THRESHOLD` (uint 10..100k) — refresh cadence
New `FlagScope::Memory` variant added to group the rolling flags
distinctly from `Llm` (rolling is useful even without an LLM
configured, via the heuristic path).

## What does not change

* No new dependency.
* Default-off: a caller who doesn't set `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY=1`
  sees byte-identical behaviour to v0.5.1.
* No new MCP tool or schema change.
* No effect on existing benchmarks (they don't set the env var).

shape is JSON (`kubectl get -o json`, `aws --output json`,
`gh api`, raw `curl`) the dispatcher routed it to `generic` which
did line-level dedup + truncate — which on JSON degrades to
"strip blank lines, hope for the best". Reality: aws/gh/kubectl-
JSON outputs were saving 0 % on the per-command bench.

## New `CompressionStrategy::JsonStructural`

```rust
JsonStructural {
    keep_first_items: usize,    // truncate arrays > N items
    max_string_chars: usize,    // clip long string values
}
```

Single-byte sniff at the start of `input.trim_start()` short-
circuits non-JSON input (so the strategy is essentially free for
plain text). When parse succeeds, `compress_json_value` recurses:

- arrays of length > `keep_first_items` → truncate to N items +
  a `"... and M more items of similar shape"` tail marker
- string values longer than `max_string_chars` → suffix-clip with
  `"… (clipped, original N chars)"`
- objects + primitives → recurse into children

Output is `serde_json::to_string_pretty` so the LLM sees structure
on multiple lines (token cost is dominated by content, not
whitespace). Parse failure → input passed through verbatim.

## Wired into 3 filters

* `generic_filter` — first strategy, before line-level passes.
  Catches anything not routed to a domain-specific filter.
* `curl_json_filter` — first strategy, before the line filter
  that keeps HTTP status + headers.
* `kubectl_get_filter` — first strategy, before column extraction.
  Tabular output passes through unchanged; `-o json` output gets
  structural compression.

## Bug fix: `budget_cap` used to destroy structured output

When `JsonStructural` ran successfully and the resulting
pretty-printed JSON exceeded `max_output_tokens`, the legacy
`budget_cap` middle-truncate kicked in and reduced 5 carefully-
preserved pods to literally `{` plus the omission marker (because
preserve_head was tuned for tabular output where a single header
line is enough).

Fix: skip `budget_cap` when `json_structural` already ran. The
JSON strategy is content-aware and produces bounded output by
construction (`keep_first_items` is a hard cap on array length),
so the line-based truncate is both unnecessary and actively
harmful here.

`compress_output_per_command.py` gains 3 JSON-heavy samples that
exercise the new path:

* `kubectl get pods -o json`        50 pods × full metadata blob
* `aws s3api list-objects-v2`        80 S3 objects + container
* `gh api .../issues`                40 issues with bodies

Aggregate (weighted, 18 commands now):

  weighted aggregate      83.1 %            **90.1 %**
  mean per-command        56.0 %            **62.4 %**
  median per-command      51.8 %            **65.8 %**

Per-command on the new samples:

feat(memory): rolling summary at update_memory time — phase 2B

Move conversation-summary cost from query time to ingest time.
With LLM summarisation enabled, compress_history was paying 5-8 s
per call to re-summarise the entire history; that's now amortised
across N=50 ingests, with the query-time path doing nothing more
than stitching the cached summary to the live recent window.

Without LLM (default zero-ML mode), the heuristic path still wins:
the older slice is summarised once when the threshold trips
instead of on every snapshot.

## API additions (`memory-manager` crate)

```rust
pub struct RollingSummary {
    pub summary: String,
    pub summarized_until: usize,         // exclusive
    pub refreshed_at: chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>,
}

pub const DEFAULT_ROLLING_REFRESH_THRESHOLD: usize = 50;

pub fn refresh_rolling_summary(
    history: &[Message],
    existing: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
    refresh_threshold: usize,
) -> Option<RollingSummary>;

pub fn compress_history_with_rolling(
    messages: &[Message],
    rolling: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
) -> CompressedMemory;
```

`refresh_rolling_summary` returns `None` below threshold or when
keeping `recent_floor = max(2 × recent_window, 8)` messages live
would consume the whole un-summarised tail. LLM activation matches
the existing `compress_history` policy (`SOPHON_LLM_CMD` implicit,
`config.use_llm_summarization` explicit, `SOPHON_NO_LLM_SUMMARY=1`
opt-out); LLM-call failure falls back to `heuristic_summarize` so
ingest never blocks on a transient subprocess error.

`compress_history_with_rolling` is strictly additive: when
`rolling` is `None` (or stale), it falls back to the existing
`compress_history` path. Output is byte-identical to the pre-2B
implementation when the feature is off.

## MemoryManager integration

* New fields: `rolling: Option<RollingSummary>`, `rolling_threshold:
  usize`, `rolling_enabled: bool`.
* `new()` reads `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY` (bool) and
  `SOPHON_ROLLING_THRESHOLD` (uint, floor 10) once at construction.
  Stored as flags rather than re-read every operation so behaviour
  stays reproducible mid-session under bench harnesses that
  toggle env vars.
* `with_persistence(path)` loads `<path>.sophon-summary.json`
  sidecar if it exists AND rolling is enabled — discards a sidecar
  ahead of the live history (e.g. JSONL truncated externally).
* `append()` calls `refresh_rolling_summary` after extending; if a
  new state is produced, persists the sidecar to disk and updates
  the in-memory `rolling` field.
* `snapshot()` routes through `compress_history_with_rolling`,
  which serves the cached summary when present.
* `reset()` clears `rolling` AND deletes the sidecar.
* New accessors: `rolling_summary()` and `rolling_enabled()` for
  diagnostics + the bench harness.

## Tests

5 new unit tests in `summarizer::rolling_tests` covering threshold
gating, recent-floor enforcement, no-op on identical input, stale
state fallback, and equivalence with the no-rolling path.

5 new integration tests in `tests/integration_test.rs` covering
default-off contract, threshold firing, snapshot path, JSONL
sidecar persistence + reload, and reset cleanup. Test functions
that touch process-global env vars are serialised via a `Mutex`
guard (`RollingEnv::enable` / `RollingEnv::disabled`) to avoid
races under cargo's parallel test runner.

## sophon doctor

Two new flags exposed in the runtime-flags table:
  * `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY` (bool) — feature toggle
  * `SOPHON_ROLLING_THRESHOLD` (uint 10..100k) — refresh cadence
New `FlagScope::Memory` variant added to group the rolling flags
distinctly from `Llm` (rolling is useful even without an LLM
configured, via the heuristic path).

## What does not change

* No new dependency.
* Default-off: a caller who doesn't set `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY=1`
  sees byte-identical behaviour to v0.5.1.
* No new MCP tool or schema change.
* No effect on existing benchmarks (they don't set the env var).

perf(release): aggressive size profile — 8.6 MB → 5.2 MB (-39 %)

The default release profile was cargo's stock (opt-level=3, lto=false,
codegen-units=16, no strip, panic=unwind). Adding a workspace-level
[profile.release] with LTO + single codegen unit + strip + abort-on-
panic shaves the v0.5.1 binary from **8.6 MB to 5.2 MB** with **zero**
cold-start regression vs the v0.5.1 baseline.

Profile chosen empirically by trying three variants:

    profile                                size      cold p50
    ------------------------------------   -------   ---------
    v0.5.1 baseline                        8.6 MB    35 ms
    opt-level="z" + lto+codegen+strip      4.0 MB    81 ms   ← rejected (perf)
    opt-level="s" + lto+codegen+strip      4.5 MB    43 ms   ← rejected (perf)
    opt-level=3   + lto+codegen+strip      5.2 MB    35 ms   ← chosen

opt-level="z"/"s" both regressed the tiktoken-rs BPE merge loop
measurably; opt-level=3 keeps the inner-loop optimizations and lets
LTO + strip do the size work via cross-crate dead-code elimination
and dropped debug symbols.

`panic = "abort"` is safe here — the workspace contains no
`catch_unwind` calls (verified via grep), and the MCP stdio
dispatcher already treats malformed-request panics as
unrecoverable: aborting on panic is strictly safer than risking
an unwinding stack mid-request, and saves the unwind tables that
were costing ~700 KB of binary.

Workspace tests stay green under the new profile (`cargo test
--workspace --release`, 380+ tests).

Phase 2A of phase-2 plan complete. No CHANGELOG entry yet —
batched into the v0.5.2 release commit later.

feat(memory): rolling summary at update_memory time — phase 2B

Move conversation-summary cost from query time to ingest time.
With LLM summarisation enabled, compress_history was paying 5-8 s
per call to re-summarise the entire history; that's now amortised
across N=50 ingests, with the query-time path doing nothing more
than stitching the cached summary to the live recent window.

Without LLM (default zero-ML mode), the heuristic path still wins:
the older slice is summarised once when the threshold trips
instead of on every snapshot.

## API additions (`memory-manager` crate)

```rust
pub struct RollingSummary {
    pub summary: String,
    pub summarized_until: usize,         // exclusive
    pub refreshed_at: chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>,
}

pub const DEFAULT_ROLLING_REFRESH_THRESHOLD: usize = 50;

pub fn refresh_rolling_summary(
    history: &[Message],
    existing: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
    refresh_threshold: usize,
) -> Option<RollingSummary>;

pub fn compress_history_with_rolling(
    messages: &[Message],
    rolling: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
) -> CompressedMemory;
```

`refresh_rolling_summary` returns `None` below threshold or when
keeping `recent_floor = max(2 × recent_window, 8)` messages live
would consume the whole un-summarised tail. LLM activation matches
the existing `compress_history` policy (`SOPHON_LLM_CMD` implicit,
`config.use_llm_summarization` explicit, `SOPHON_NO_LLM_SUMMARY=1`
opt-out); LLM-call failure falls back to `heuristic_summarize` so
ingest never blocks on a transient subprocess error.

`compress_history_with_rolling` is strictly additive: when
`rolling` is `None` (or stale), it falls back to the existing
`compress_history` path. Output is byte-identical to the pre-2B
implementation when the feature is off.

perf: tracing spans on hot path + tokenizer warm-up + embedding reuse

Three phase-1 gains that ship together because they all live on the
same perf surface.

## tracing::instrument on the 5 hot-path entries

Adds `#[instrument(skip_all, fields(...))]` with structured fields
to:
  * memory_manager::compress_history       (messages, max_tokens, recent_window)
  * prompt_compressor::compress_prompt     (sections, max_tokens, has_semantic_scores)
  * output_compressor::OutputCompressor::compress
                                           (command, input_chars)
                                           + DEBUG-level "compress_output result"
                                           with filter / strategies / ratio
  * semantic_retriever::Retriever::retrieve
                                           (query_chars, top_k, min_score,
                                            store_len, hybrid, multihop)
  * semantic_retriever::Retriever::index_messages
                                           (messages, embedder, hybrid)

Zero runtime cost when RUST_LOG is off (tracing compiles the whole
span to a no-op). With `RUST_LOG=sophon=debug` the agent-session
timeline becomes trivially scriptable. Added `tracing` dep to the
two remaining crates (prompt-compressor, semantic-retriever).

## Eager tokenizer warm-up at `sophon` startup

Added `warm_up_tokenizer()` — one `count_tokens("warmup")` call
right after `init_tracing()`. Loads tiktoken-rs BPE merge tables
into memory at startup instead of on the first real call.

Measured on the scaling curve bench (200 turns, checkpoint 25):

                      before (v0.5.0)   after (this commit)
  update_memory p99       30.5 ms            0.4 ms      (~75x)
  compress_history p99    50.4 ms           49.2 ms      (~flat)
  RSS idle                12.5 MB           41.6 MB      (+29 MB loaded upfront)
  RSS after 100 calls     42.0 MB           41.8 MB      (+0.2 MB)

The RSS bump is the tokenizer tables that were previously allocated
lazily on first call — we now pay it once at boot instead of
spiking the first request.

## JSONL store embedding reuse

`Retriever::open` previously re-embedded every stored chunk on
load. At 1k chunks this is ~10 ms; at 100k it's multi-second. The
chunk already carries `Option<Vec<f32>>` and `index_messages`
already populates it — we just weren't consuming the persisted
vector on reopen.

New loop in `with_embedder` reuses `chunk.embedding` when its
dimension matches the current embedder (i.e. user didn't switch
from hash → bge mid-session) and only falls back to
`embedder.embed(chunk.content)` otherwise. Emits a DEBUG tracing
line with the reused / re-embedded counters.

Guarded by a new e2e integration test
(`e2e_cached_embeddings_survive_reopen_and_match_freshly_computed`)
that asserts the top-chunk score is bit-identical before and after
close/reopen. HashEmbedder is deterministic so re-embedding would
also pass — but the CPU work is now skipped.

messages.content: Walk me through commit 41b6076.

feat(memory): rolling summary at update_memory time — phase 2B

Move conversation-summary cost from query time to ingest time.
With LLM summarisation enabled, compress_history was paying 5-8 s
per call to re-summarise the entire history; that's now amortised
across N=50 ingests, with the query-time path doing nothing more
than stitching the cached summary to the live recent window.

Without LLM (default zero-ML mode), the heuristic path still wins:
the older slice is summarised once when the threshold trips
instead of on every snapshot.

## API additions (`memory-manager` crate)

```rust
pub struct RollingSummary {
    pub summary: String,
    pub summarized_until: usize,         // exclusive
    pub refreshed_at: chrono::DateTime<chrono::Utc>,
}

pub const DEFAULT_ROLLING_REFRESH_THRESHOLD: usize = 50;

pub fn refresh_rolling_summary(
    history: &[Message],
    existing: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
    refresh_threshold: usize,
) -> Option<RollingSummary>;

pub fn compress_history_with_rolling(
    messages: &[Message],
    rolling: Option<&RollingSummary>,
    config: &MemoryConfig,
) -> CompressedMemory;
```

`refresh_rolling_summary` returns `None` below threshold or when
keeping `recent_floor = max(2 × recent_window, 8)` messages live
would consume the whole un-summarised tail. LLM activation matches
the existing `compress_history` policy (`SOPHON_LLM_CMD` implicit,
`config.use_llm_summarization` explicit, `SOPHON_NO_LLM_SUMMARY=1`
opt-out); LLM-call failure falls back to `heuristic_summarize` so
ingest never blocks on a transient subprocess error.

`compress_history_with_rolling` is strictly additive: when
`rolling` is `None` (or stale), it falls back to the existing
`compress_history` path. Output is byte-identical to the pre-2B
implementation when the feature is off.

## MemoryManager integration

* New fields: `rolling: Option<RollingSummary>`, `rolling_threshold:
  usize`, `rolling_enabled: bool`.
* `new()` reads `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY` (bool) and
  `SOPHON_ROLLING_THRESHOLD` (uint, floor 10) once at construction.
  Stored as flags rather than re-read every operation so behaviour
  stays reproducible mid-session under bench harnesses that
  toggle env vars.
* `with_persistence(path)` loads `<path>.sophon-summary.json`
  sidecar if it exists AND rolling is enabled — discards a sidecar
  ahead of the live history (e.g. JSONL truncated externally).
* `append()` calls `refresh_rolling_summary` after extending; if a
  new state is produced, persists the sidecar to disk and updates
  the in-memory `rolling` field.
* `snapshot()` routes through `compress_history_with_rolling`,
  which serves the cached summary when present.
* `reset()` clears `rolling` AND deletes the sidecar.
* New accessors: `rolling_summary()` and `rolling_enabled()` for
  diagnostics + the bench harness.

## Tests

5 new unit tests in `summarizer::rolling_tests` covering threshold
gating, recent-floor enforcement, no-op on identical input, stale
state fallback, and equivalence with the no-rolling path.

5 new integration tests in `tests/integration_test.rs` covering
default-off contract, threshold firing, snapshot path, JSONL
sidecar persistence + reload, and reset cleanup. Test functions
that touch process-global env vars are serialised via a `Mutex`
guard (`RollingEnv::enable` / `RollingEnv::disabled`) to avoid
races under cargo's parallel test runner.

## sophon doctor

Two new flags exposed in the runtime-flags table:
  * `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY` (bool) — feature toggle
  * `SOPHON_ROLLING_THRESHOLD` (uint 10..100k) — refresh cadence
New `FlagScope::Memory` variant added to group the rolling flags
distinctly from `Llm` (rolling is useful even without an LLM
configured, via the heuristic path).

## What does not change

* No new dependency.
* Default-off: a caller who doesn't set `SOPHON_ROLLING_SUMMARY=1`
  sees byte-identical behaviour to v0.5.1.
* No new MCP tool or schema change.
* No effect on existing benchmarks (they don't set the env var).

perf(release): aggressive size profile — 8.6 MB → 5.2 MB (-39 %)

The default release profile was cargo's stock (opt-level=3, lto=false,
codegen-units=16, no strip, panic=unwind). Adding a workspace-level
[profile.release] with LTO + single codegen unit + strip + abort-on-
panic shaves the v0.5.1 binary from **8.6 MB to 5.2 MB** with **zero**
cold-start regression vs the v0.5.1 baseline.

Profile chosen empirically by trying three variants:

    profile                                size      cold p50
    ------------------------------------   -------   ---------
    v0.5.1 baseline                        8.6 MB    35 ms
    opt-level="z" + lto+codegen+strip      4.0 MB    81 ms   ← rejected (perf)
    opt-level="s" + lto+codegen+strip      4.5 MB    43 ms   ← rejected (perf)
    opt-level=3   + lto+codegen+strip      5.2 MB    35 ms   ← chosen

opt-level="z"/"s" both regressed the tiktoken-rs BPE merge loop
measurably; opt-level=3 keeps the inner-loop optimizations and lets
LTO + strip do the size work via cross-crate dead-code elimination
and dropped debug symbols.

`panic = "abort"` is safe here — the workspace contains no
`catch_unwind` calls (verified via grep), and the MCP stdio
dispatcher already treats malformed-request panics as
unrecoverable: aborting on panic is strictly safer than risking
an unwinding stack mid-request, and saves the unwind tables that
were costing ~700 KB of binary.

Workspace tests stay green under the new profile (`cargo test
--workspace --release`, 380+ tests).

Phase 2A of phase-2 plan complete. No CHANGELOG entry yet —
batched into the v0.5.2 release commit later.

feat(output): curl_verbose filter + git_diff dedup — phase 1 compression gains

Two targeted improvements driven directly by the v0.5.0
compress_output per-command bench, which surfaced two anomalous
outliers at ~0.5 % and ~11.8 % saved while the weighted aggregate
sat at 81.6 %.

## New `curl_verbose` filter

`curl -v` / `curl --verbose` output is dominated by `*`-prefixed
TLS handshake and certificate-chain noise that is ~0 % useful to
an LLM. The existing `curl_json` filter treated `*` lines as
signal (keep pattern `^[<>*]`) — correct for `-i` headers, wrong
for `-v`.

New filter matches strictly:
    ^\s*curl\b.*\s-v(?:\s|$)
    ^\s*curl\b.*\s--verbose\b
    ^\s*curl\b.*\s--trace(?:-ascii|-ids|-time)?\b

and drops `*` lines except the outcome marker ("Connection #0
left intact"), while preserving `> GET ...`, `< HTTP/... STATUS`,
`< Header: value`, and the response body.

Registered **ahead of** `curl_json` in the filter registry so the
stricter match wins. Plain `curl URL` (no `-v`) still routes to
`curl_json` — guarded by a dispatcher test
(`plain_curl_still_routes_to_curl_json`).

Measured on the per-command bench:
    curl -v ...  :  0.5 % → 60.3 % saved  (+59.8 pt)

## `git_diff` dedup strategy

Bulk refactors (rename, import reorder, signature change repeated
across N call sites) produce diffs with identical `-old` / `+new`
hunk pairs. The pipeline now runs `CompressionStrategy::Deduplicate`
with `similarity_threshold=1.0` (exact match only, no fuzzy merge)
between the line-filter and truncate passes. Collapses runs of
identical consecutive lines to `<line>  // (× N)`.

Doesn't touch semantically distinct hunks — only crushes literal
repetition from mechanical changes.

Measured:
    git diff HEAD~3  :  11.8 % → 51.8 % saved  (+40.0 pt)

## Aggregate

Rerun of `benchmarks/compress_output_per_command.py` over the same
15 canned samples:

                         before         after
  weighted aggregate     81.6 %         83.1 %
  mean per-command       49.4 %         56.0 %
  median per-command     48.4 %         51.8 %

Only the two targeted commands moved; every other row is identical.
Registry test count bumped from 20 → 21 filters; new dispatcher
tests assert verbose routes ahead of json while plain curl stays
on the json path.

perf: tracing spans on hot path + tokenizer warm-up + embedding reuse

Three phase-1 gains that ship together because they all live on the
same perf surface.

## tracing::instrument on the 5 hot-path entries

Adds `#[instrument(skip_all, fields(...))]` with structured fields
to:
  * memory_manager::compress_history       (messages, max_tokens, recent_window)
  * prompt_compressor::compress_prompt     (sections, max_tokens, has_semantic_scores)
  * output_compressor::OutputCompressor::compress
                                           (command, input_chars)
                                           + DEBUG-level "compress_output result"
                                           with filter / strategies / ratio
  * semantic_retriever::Retriever::retrieve
                                           (query_chars, top_k, min_score,
                                            store_len, hybrid, multihop)
  * semantic_retriever::Retriever::index_messages
                                           (messages, embedder, hybrid)

Zero runtime cost when RUST_LOG is off (tracing compiles the whole
span to a no-op). With `RUST_LOG=sophon=debug` the agent-session
timeline becomes trivially scriptable. Added `tracing` dep to the
two remaining crates (prompt-compressor, semantic-retriever).

## Eager tokenizer warm-up at `sophon` startup

Added `warm_up_tokenizer()` — one `count_tokens("warmup")` call
right after `init_tracing()`. Loads tiktoken-rs BPE merge tables
into memory at startup instead of on the first real call.

Measured on the scaling curve bench (200 turns, checkpoint 25):

                      before (v0.5.0)   after (this commit)
  update_memory p99       30.5 ms            0.4 ms      (~75x)
  compress_history p99    50.4 ms           49.2 ms      (~flat)
  RSS idle                12.5 MB           41.6 MB      (+29 MB loaded upfront)
  RSS after 100 calls     42.0 MB           41.8 MB      (+0.2 MB)

The RSS bump is the tokenizer tables that were previously allocated
lazily on first call — we now pay it once at boot instead of
spiking the first request.

## JSONL store embedding reuse

`Retriever::open` previously re-embedded every stored chunk on
load. At 1k chunks this is ~10 ms; at 100k it's multi-second. The
chunk already carries `Option<Vec<f32>>` and `index_messages`
already populates it — we just weren't consuming the persisted
vector on reopen.

New loop in `with_embedder` reuses `chunk.embedding` when its
dimension matches the current embedder (i.e. user didn't switch
from hash → bge mid-session) and only falls back to
`embedder.embed(chunk.content)` otherwise. Emits a DEBUG tracing
line with the reused / re-embedded counters.

Guarded by a new e2e integration test
(`e2e_cached_embeddings_survive_reopen_and_match_freshly_computed`)
that asserts the top-chunk score is bit-identical before and after
close/reopen. HashEmbedder is deterministic so re-embedding would
also pass — but the CPU work is now skipped.

feat(output): curl_verbose filter + git_diff dedup — phase 1 compression gains

Two targeted improvements driven directly by the v0.5.0
compress_output per-command bench, which surfaced two anomalous
outliers at ~0.5 % and ~11.8 % saved while the weighted aggregate
sat at 81.6 %.

## New `curl_verbose` filter

`curl -v` / `curl --verbose` output is dominated by `*`-prefixed
TLS handshake and certificate-chain noise that is ~0 % useful to
an LLM. The existing `curl_json` filter treated `*` lines as
signal (keep pattern `^[<>*]`) — correct for `-i` headers, wrong
for `-v`.

New filter matches strictly:
    ^\s*curl\b.*\s-v(?:\s|$)
    ^\s*curl\b.*\s--verbose\b
    ^\s*curl\b.*\s--trace(?:-ascii|-ids|-time)?\b

and drops `*` lines except the outcome marker ("Connection #0
left intact"), while preserving `> GET ...`, `< HTTP/... STATUS`,
`< Header: value`, and the response body.

stricter match wins. Plain `curl URL` (no `-v`) still routes to
`curl_json` — guarded by a dispatcher test
